core: working definition: business communication is the exchange of information inside a business (coworkers, teams, departments) and between the business and the outside world (customers, suppliers, investors, the public), built on CFI's definition of communication ('transferring information to produce greater understanding') and Business Communication for Success ('the process of understanding and sharing meaning')

why it matters: poor communication causes misunderstandings and frustration, which cost time and money; the general argument is supported by CFI and illustrated with an original example (the cleaning-company email)
channels named with one-line fits: email, meetings, reports, presentations, instant messages
clear writing basics: audience, purpose, structure, plain language
listening and feedback: communication is two-way; feedback from the receiver completes the exchange
tone and professionalism: tone is the attitude a message conveys toward the reader and subject, and it shapes the impression the message makes
the honest framing: the best business communication is the clearest, not the longest
supporting: CFI: from a business standpoint, all transactions result from communication; choosing the right medium matters (serious matters in person, not by email)
CFI: lack of specific communication is a sign of poor communication; active listening means paying close attention and clarifying by rephrasing
Purdue OWL: audience determines form, genre, and tone; concise, clear, jargon-free, positive business writing
Purdue OWL: tone in writing is the writer's attitude toward the reader and the subject, affecting how the reader perceives the message
outOfScope: sales — sibling topic owns selling and customer persuasion
leadership — sibling topic owns motivating people
human-resources — sibling topic owns internal employee communications (onboarding, policy messaging)
marketing — sibling topic owns promotion and advertising
nonverbal communication and body language in depth — mentioned only in passing
negotiation, public-speaking technique, and crisis communication — related skills not taught here

claims.claim: Corporate Finance Institute (CFI) defines communication as transferring information to produce greater understanding.

Business Communication for Success (Saylor Foundation adaptation) defines communication as the process of understanding and sharing meaning, and treats communication as a process rather than a one-time event.

The lesson's working definition — business communication is the exchange of information inside a business and between the business and the outside world — is its own framing built on the two attributed definitions.
From a business standpoint, all transactions result from communication; poor communication skills lead to frequent misunderstandings and frustration (CFI).
Choosing the right medium matters: serious matters such as layoffs or salary changes are more appropriately communicated in person than by email (CFI).
Lack of specific communication is a sign of poor communication and a source of workplace problems (CFI).

Active listening — paying close attention and clarifying by rephrasing — is part of effective communication (CFI); feedback or response from the audience is part of the communication process (Business Communication for Success).
Different audiences have different expectations of form, genre, and tone, so business writers must adapt their writing to their audience (Purdue OWL).
Business writing should be concise, clear, easy to read, and free of technical jargon, and should use a confident, positive tone (Purdue OWL).
Tone in writing refers to the writer's attitude toward the reader and the subject of the message, and it affects how the reader perceives the message (Purdue OWL).

Conciseness means conveying the message in as few words as possible; rambling makes the listener tune out or lose the point (CFI) — the basis of the lesson's honest framing that the clearest message, not the longest, is best.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether communication is one-way information transfer or a shared-meaning process
positions: CFI defines communication as transferring information to produce greater understanding — a transfer framing.
Business Communication for Success defines communication as the process of understanding and sharing meaning, emphasizing the receiver's role and feedback.
Some workplace portrayals treat sending a message as the whole job.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson builds its working definition on both attributed definitions and teaches the two-way view: sending is only half, and feedback from the receiver completes the exchange.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether email is acceptable for serious news
positions: Email is fast and convenient, and some organizations send major announcements by email.
CFI notes that serious matters such as layoffs and salary changes are more appropriately communicated in person, citing the widely criticized 2006 RadioShack email layoff notices as an example.
The lesson teaches the general principle that serious, personal news belongs in a direct conversation, without presenting it as a universal or legal rule.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents channel choice as judgment: match the medium to the seriousness of the message, with in-person preferred for sensitive news.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether longer messages are more thorough or more harmful
positions: Some writers add detail out of fear of leaving something out.
CFI and Purdue OWL both teach concision: say it in as few words as possible, highlight the important points early, and avoid rambling.
The lesson adopts the concision view as its honest framing: the clearest message, not the longest, is the best.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches that completeness means including the essential specifics, not adding words; detail must serve understanding.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The phase-2 generated draft for this topic contained no factual claims — only generic boilerplate ('Business Communication is a foundational concept in Introduction To Business'); none of its wording was carried into the lesson.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic machine-generated draft entirely with source-verified content.
Built and attributed the working definition of business communication to CFI and Business Communication for Success instead of leaving the concept undefined.
